Concerns About Canoe Tripping 


following a number of tragic canoeing and tripping accidents in Canada, 
the Society of Camp Directors became alarmed to hear of the number of organi¬ 
zations and associations which initiated plans to establish yet more sets of 
standards and rules which many felt should then be imposed on camps and in¬ 
terested groups of trippers. 

There seemed to be little direction or concerted purpose in these de¬ 
liberations. The Society felt that perhaps our greatest contribution to wil¬ 
derness travel safety in this country would be to gather information as to 
the practices which presently exist in Canadian Camps. About 120 question¬ 
naires were sent out to camps, resident, agency, church, outdoor education 
centres, tripping businesses and private camps. About 60 responses were re¬ 
ceived from camps which stated they were mostly resident and offered mixed 
activities. The majority of respondents were members of the Ontario Camping 
Association, although eight provinces were represented. Most of the camps 
had campers beginning at eight years of age. The majority of camps carried 
on tripping in big or small lakes, rivers or remote countryside. 

The type of tripping done was broken down into four categories. They 

were: 

short trips - one or two nights 
moderate trips - three to five nights 
long trips - six to nine nights 
extended trips - ten or more nights 

A large part of the questionnaire dealt with trip leadership and assis¬ 
tant leadership. Table I gives the reader a summary of the qualifications 
expected by camp leaders of their leaders in charge. The responses listed 
(and in order of appearance if more than one) are the responses which were 
most often received to the question concerned. For example at the beginning 
of the questionnaire, 38 camps state that they use the Red Cross System for 
swimming qualification, 29 use the Royal Life Saving Society System, and 8 
use the Y.M.C.A. System. Yet 36 camps stated they required their leader in 
charge of a short canoe trip to have a Bronze Medallion (R.L.S.S.). This 
occurs frequently with the swimming qualifications.

TRIPPING 


The canoeing standards expected of leaders in charge were more varied. We 
have provincial, national and international standards. Yet most camps expected 
their leaders to have canoeing experience or pass a test set by the camp. Some 
camps submitted these camp standards with the returned questionnaire, but the 
author felt he was not in a position to relate these to established standards. 


For other qualifications expected of the leader in charge, we have below 
a list which is compiled from all the respondents. As we have no standards 
(except First Aid) it serves as a handy check list of qualifications you may 
want to consider.

The best prevention for accidents is probably discussion of possible ac¬ 
cidents, according to camp directors. Next they preferred instruction. Such 
things they either discussed or instructed upon in pre-camp are: (the top ones 
being the most popular etc.) 

Physical accidents 
First Aid 
Inclement Weather 
Hypothermia 
Missing camper 
Loss of Canoe 
Fire 

Animal hazards 

Serious danger to canoes and equipment 

Navigational skills 

Loss of food packs 

Missing staff member 

intruders 

Emergency use of private property 

Evacuation/search/rescue 

Illness 

Coldness 

Interference by motor boats 
Swim skills 

Most of these above eventualities were also discussed with campers prior 
to a trip. For many these were also included as part of the campcraft program. 

An issue that was just brushed on brought most interesting results. That 
is the handling of emotional stress brought on to campers as a result of their 
new situation and as a reflection of the environment they came from. There were 
two opinions. One was that directors did not really cover this aspect in pre- 
camp, and expected their staff to be on top of this. The other group did dis¬ 
cuss it but suggested that probably they did not do it justice.

Tables IV and V again reflect the most important considerations of camp 
directors. In each case, the qualifications expected of campers are a reflec¬ 
tion of the camp T s own policies. 


In the majority of camps, campers are checked medically before camp. 

However only half require their campers to be checked by the camp nurse before 
departing on a trip. In all cases the trip leader is aware of the campers health 
Most camps do not check for weight gain or loss during a trip. And all camps 
advise their campers on suitable trip apparel before camp opens. All camps 
expect their campers to bring sleeping bags, although only half expect them to 
bring ground sheets or lifejackets. Even less expect the campers to bring mess 

kits, paddles or blanket rolls. 

About a third of the camps maintain a standard that 

makes wearing a lifejacket mandatory on trips. Others 
just expect it in rough weather, when the 
_ . - - leader deems it, or for campers 

who have not met a certain 
prerequisite. 





In descending order of importance canoe trip equipment included, first 
aid boxes, water purifiers, touring ropes, stern lines, bailers, swede saw, 
spades, long handled axe, wanigans and hatchets. Many camp directors expressed 
the concern away from the use of hatchets or axes, stating that there is usual¬ 
ly enough brush available. Types of bailers included cans, cups, javex bottles, 
plastic containers, sponges, billy cans, pots and buckets. Most camps allowed 
their campers to bring their own knives, and in many cases there were restrictions 
on the hows, whys and where they were to be used. Two thirds of the camps still 
use the canvas canoe; half , the aluminum or fibreglass. Few are using the newer 
plastic models. Standard 16 or 17 foot canoes are the favourite although a few 
camps used the longer "war canoe" types which hold more campers. Half the camps 
stated that there must be one spare paddle per canoe. The types of shelter fa¬ 
voured in descending order were: 3 person tents; weatherproof, 4 (or more) per- 
sontents; 2 person tents; fire retardant tents; poleless and self-contained tents. 
Opinions seemed to be varied as to the use of dehydrated or freeze dried foods. 

No clear trend emerged. This alone would be an interesting study as to possible 
reasons why. 

By and large, campers sign up for the trips and are assigned trips ac¬ 
cording to experience or grouping. Practise time for the group varied from a 
J day to a canoe school at the first stop. In the majority of cases campers 
were quite involved in route and menu planning; packing and the program of the 
trip. 

All staff were familiar with methods of con¬ 
tacting camp which seemed to be the pnone. Many, 
many other methods of contact were indicated, ac¬ 
cording to the locale. The trip group in two- 
thirds of the camps did meet with the director 
before departure.

The above TABLE IV reflects the most popular number of participants per 
trip. In all cases, three people per canoe was the most favoured. Canoeists 
are by and large instructed to stay together before and after portages and on 
the trip. Methods of portaging varied, the most common methods (paddles, tumps 
and yokes) being used. 

Most camps preferred to use existing campsites, establishing new ones on¬ 
ly when necessary. Campsite arrangement is optional to according to standards 
established by the camp. In most cases garbage is burned and carried out. 

If a canoe trip could not leave from the camp property, the majority of 
camps kept travelling to a minimum, used their own trailers and vans and encour¬ 
aged resting, a meal or an overnight at or near the drop off point. In these 
cases, canoe trips had pre-arranged time schedules and pick up points which 
were changed only if communicated by the trip leader. For longer trips, a 
one in five day rest day seems to be a built in part of the trip. Night tripping 
was not favoured by most camp directors. 

Most camps discouraged visits to other camps or visits to towns. In the 
latter cases, restrictions are enforced. Most camps do not allow campers to 
smoke on trips. Staff smoking was of divided opinion, those in favour encour¬ 
aging precaution and responsibility to themselves, the environment and campers. 
Alcohol was overwhelmingly rejected for staff on trips. 


Below is a list of the most favoured objectives of canoe tripping at all 
levels: 

Learn camp skills Canoe sailing 

Nature study Survival camping 

Exploration Solo camping 

Fishing Rock climbing 

Astronomy Caving 

Only 15 camps maintained that white water canoeing is an integral part 
of the camp program. Whitewater, for many, was handled briefly before a trip 
and dealt with again if it arose. In most cases packs were secured. The fol¬ 
lowing are some of the skills taught: 

River reading Lining and tracking 

Position in white water after upset Rescue procedures 

Scouting the shore Eddy turns 

High and low braces 

As follow up, more camps have their equipment checked by the trip lea¬ 
der after each trip. Logs are kept for future occasions, evaluations of cam¬ 
pers for post camp evaluations, staff evaluations for future reference, are 
all carried on in some form or other. 

Of the many values camp directors hope to impart to the young canoeist, 
below are the most popular: 

coping with the new experience 
enj oyment 

instruction in basic camp craft and canoeing 
cooperation 

environmental awareness And for the older campers; 

develop group living skills develop physical and technical skills 

small group association with challenge 

cooperation 

ecological concern 

appreciation for outdoor living 

friendship 

Finally, we asked camp directors if they had any concerns on the matter 
of canoe tripping in camps. The May 1980 issue of M Canadian Camping 11 lists 
46 comments pulled from many lengthy comments. 

Inconclusion, the questionnaire and the tabulated responses can be ob¬ 
tained from the C.C.A. office. The Society of Camp Directors and myself 
would like to thank those who helped start this project, and those who respon¬ 
ded. Also particular thanks must be given Mary Northway and the Neathern Trust 
for their moral and financial support. 

Respectfully submitted, 

Mike Hoyer 

Michael Hoyer is an Assistant Camp Director of Camp Oconto
